reason: Attacked and not broken. The verifier's fetch of the course PDF failed to render, so I did not inherit its reading: I decompressed the PDF's streams myself and pulled the text-showing operators out to plain text. The document's own head reads 'Flannery O'Connor / Mystery and Manners: Occasional Prose / edited by Sally and Robert Fitzgerald / The Nature and Aim of Fiction', so the reproduction names the edition and the essay, and the essay text follows whole, opening 'I understand that this is a course called How the Writer Writes'. Both sentences stand verbatim in it: 'The writer should never be ashamed of staring. There is nothing that doesn't require his attention.' They close the paragraph whose last three sentences run 'Any discipline can help your writing: logic, mathematics, theology, and of course and particularly drawing. Anything that helps you to see, anything that makes you look. The writer should never be ashamed of staring. There is nothing that doesn't require his attention.' The next words in the file begin a new paragraph, 'We hear a great deal of lamentation these days about writers having all taken themselves to the colleges', so the quotation ends at a real paragraph break and mints nothing. One correction to the evidence, not to the card: the paragraph does not begin at 'Any discipline can help your writing', it begins at 'I don't know which is worse to have a bad teacher or no teacher at all'; the two sentences do close it, which is what matters. The verifier was right to refuse the page number. Two secondary citations put the neighbouring sentence at p. 84 and the Internet Archive scan is lending restricted, so no page is claimed and none should be; the essay title is a locator in its own right under the rule that allows work plus section. Attribution: O'Connor's own signed prose, not a character, so no speaker is owed, and it is on no line of the misattribution list. Scope: a named work by a named author, 1969, not scripture, film, lyric, proverb or business. shipped.js returns shipped [], near [], person 'flannery oconnor', yearCount 0, atCap false, banned false, run before proposing and again before ruling. Mechanics: the source line leads with the name, has no dash, no straight double quote, and runs 103 characters; the quotation ends in a full stop and uses a curly apostrophe in doesn't; it is prose and is not broken into lines. Tag Essay is the form of the work, Mystery and Manners being occasional prose. Publishable, and looking without flinching is Truth and Clarity exactly. Two soft spots worth naming, neither a refutation. First, the essay was assembled by the Fitzgeralds from O'Connor's talks and the text addresses a room, 'what I should say to you tonight', so a very strict reading of the out of scope line on speeches and oratory could be aimed at it; that exclusion belongs to the Makers' lane of public addresses, and a craft lecture printed as an essay in a named prose collection is an essay, which is how the Wilde and Montaigne carry-ins are already handled. Second, the text is a course reproduction rather than a scan of the book; it credits the Fitzgerald edition and the wording it carries is the wording every secondary citation carries, so the risk of a retyping drift is small but not nil. Confidence high on wording and attribution, medium only on the physical page.
